title: The Psalms
hookLine: one hundred and fifty songs linked to David, woven through every Jewish prayer service

lines: A BUS, A GRAVESIDE, A WEDDING.
cards: Walk into a hospital waiting room in Jerusalem and you may see someone rocking gently over a small book, lips moving. On a bus, a teenager doing the same. At a graveside, a whole family.
At a wedding, a grandmother. It's very often the same book.

Not the prayer book, not the Torah scroll: a collection of one hundred and fifty ancient songs, the one part of the Bible that Jews carry with them almost everywhere. For the next two weeks, let's open it.

teach.b: Tehillim is the Hebrew name for the Book of Psalms. It means praises, from the same root as hallelujah. There are one hundred and fifty, gathered into five smaller books.
An old midrash notices the pattern: Moses gave Israel five books of Torah, and David gave Israel five books of Psalms.
Jewish tradition links the Psalms to King David, the shepherd who played the harp. But the book is honest that it isn't only his.
Some psalms are headed for Asaph, some for the sons of Korah, two for Solomon, and Psalm ninety is called a prayer of Moses. Many have no name at all. What's in them?

Everything. Praise and thanks, but also fear, anger, loneliness, guilt, homesickness, questions that sound almost like accusations. "I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise shall continually be in my mouth."
And in the same book: why do You hide Your face? That range is why people reach for them. Whatever you're feeling, a psalm has already felt it.
And Jewish prayer is full of them.
The morning service opens with a stretch of psalms. Friday night welcomes Shabbat with psalms.
Festivals have their own psalms of praise, and each day of the week has its own. Coming up: the tree by the stream, the shepherd, the clean hands, the rivers of Babylon.

how: Psalms fill the Jewish prayer book, from the morning service to Friday night; many Jews also recite Tehillim privately, in times of trouble, for the sick, and at gravesides.

games.q: you're sitting in a hospital waiting room, worried and with no words of your own. what do many Jews reach for?
games.why: the Psalms are the book Jews carry almost everywhere, because there's one for every feeling.

practice: Find a short psalm in a Bible or on your phone: Psalm one hundred seventeen, the shortest in the whole book, is just two verses. Read it out loud, slowly, even in a whisper, then once more, and hear ancient words in your own voice.
If you don't have one nearby, sit with the line you heard, at all times, praise; and if you pray, make the psalm your prayer.
